lines.li: [us] What is the copper pin on your collar?
[them] From the first coil Ennis Calloway carried over the hills when the long war cut the roads.
[us] What did he do with it?
[them] He raised a mast on every height he could climb, until one valley could hear the next.
[us] And the first one?
[them] Still standing on its ridge, and it has never once gone quiet.
[them] Every message on the line is passed on true, and with where it was heard.
[us] Why does where matter?
[them] Because a thing told with the mast it was heard at is news, and without one it is rumour.
[us] And if a message is wrong?
[them] Then the line says so, and says where it went wrong.
[us] Aren't you afraid up a mast in a storm?
[them] No, silence is the only storm we fear.
[us] Why silence?
[them] Because when the masts went quiet in the war, every town thought it was alone.
[us] What does a lineman do all day?
[them] Walk the line, climb the masts, and mend what the wind broke.
[us] And the operators?
[them] They listen, and pass it on, and sell what is worth selling.
[us] Why does everyone wear the red band?
[them] Because of the night the seam under Deepwell ran dry and the owners fled.
[us] What happened that night?
[them] Marta Grieve called us all into the hall and put it to the vote, scatter or stay together.
[us] And you stayed.
[them] We wrote every name in a book and walked out with our picks the next morning.
[them] A seam worked well, a shaft shored right, and everyone up at the end of the shift.
[us] That's all of it?
[them] That's all of it, and it is harder than it sounds.
[us] And if someone doesn't come up?
[them] Then the whole union goes down after them.
[us] What does a miner fear?
[them] A cave-in, and a boss who decides alone.
[us] The second as much as the first?
[them] More, because a cave-in is quick and a bad boss is slow.
[us] Do you only dig for yourselves?
[them] We drill anyone's deep ground for a share of what comes up.
[us] And who decides the share?
[them] The union, by vote, and it is always two in five.
[us] Who governs the Republic now?
[them] The same laws that always did, read out first by Clement Ashdown, the postmaster.
[us] A postmaster?
[them] He was the most senior official left on the radio the winter the capital went dark.
[us] What did he do?
[them] He read out the old laws each evening and called an election, and other towns answered.
[them] Everyone counted, everyone owed: that is the whole of the Republic.
[us] Owed what?
[them] Its protection, its rations and its vote, and the Republic is owed a duty in return.
[us] And the uncounted?
[them] They are not forgotten, only waiting for the census.
[us] Has the Republic really never fallen?
[them] It simply has fewer citizens than it used to.
[us] What would make it fall?
[them] A silent radio, because a government that stops speaking stops being one.
[us] What do the clerks do in the town hall?
[them] Count, file, stamp and broadcast, and there is a form for that.
[us] For what?
[them] For whatever you were about to ask.
[us] Why do you still keep watches in a ship that cannot fly?
[them] Because of the last order Captain Imre Sallow gave when the hull came down.
[us] What was it?
[them] To keep our posts until the order came to disembark.
[us] And it never came?
[them] He died before he could give it, and nobody since has had the rank.
[them] Every watch is logged, every day for two hundred years.
[us] What does the log say?
[them] Most days, only that the ship is holding position.
[us] Why write it, then?
[them] So that when the order comes, it finds us at our posts.
[us] What does the crew fear most?
[them] The last part failing, and a sleeper who wakes to strangers.
[us] Do the sleepers still wake?
[them] Now and then, and we have nothing to tell them but the date.
[us] What does the Fleet trade for?
[them] Plating, parts, and anything that fell from the sky that the ship can use.
[us] And then it flies?
[them] One plate at a time, we were promised a world.
